web_evidence.title: Lost Horizon by James Hilton, from Project Gutenberg Canada
web_evidence.note: Complete text based on the 1936 Macmillan edition: the Prologue uses participating I/we narration, the narrator receives Rutherford's manuscript, Chapters I-XI narrate Conway in third person, and the Epilogue returns to the first-person frame.

web_evidence.title: James Hilton Writing Styles in The Lost Horizon
web_evidence.note: Its point-of-view section explicitly identifies the Prologue and Epilogue as first person and the rest of the novel as third-person, Conway-centered narration.

web_evidence.title: Lost Horizon Literary Elements
web_evidence.note: The narrator-and-point-of-view section explicitly describes the frame story as first person and the inner story as third person.

Searched: "Lost Horizon James Hilton frame narrative first person third person point of view" and "Lost Horizon James Hilton excerpt first chapter publisher"; opened the BookRags point-of-view page.
Searched: "Lost Horizon narrative structure prologue epilogue Rutherford scholarly"; results included irrelevant scholarship and an inaccessible PDF, neither used as evidence.

Opened the PinkMonkey sample study guide; it corroborated the frame/manuscript transition, but its point-of-view sentence was truncated, so it was not retained as web evidence. Novelguide and a full-text PDF mirror initially returned access errors.
person_note: The eleven-chapter main narrative is sustained third-person narration centered on Conway. A participating neurologist speaks in the Prologue and Epilogue, but those brief framing bookends are not a co-controlling base strand under the clarified aggregation rule. Dialogue and other local first-person material likewise do not alter the book-level result, so the base narration is THIRD.
